newsitem.title: UK: De Beers sees Europe retail remaining mixed.
newsitem.headline: De Beers sees Europe retail remaining mixed.

text.p: South African diamond giant De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd said on Wednesday that it expects conditions in the European retail diamond market will remain mixed for the rest of the year.

It also expects a difficult year for Japan, the second largest market after the U.S., although the company said it is seeing signs of economic improvement there, which it hopes will filter through to the diamond market.

"We are beginning to get one or two signs that Japan is picking up in a macro economic way and once that happens we would hope the diamond market would follow," Tim Capon, a director of De Beers and its Central Selling Organisation (CSO), told Reuters.
Capon mainly blamed the devaluation of the Japanese yen for the decline in the average value of diamond jewellery rather than a decrease in the number of people buying jewellery in Japan.
De Beers earlier announced that sales in the first six months of 1997 rose 4.81 percent to $2.88 billion.

It said that the sale of rough diamonds, through the CSO, "reflected the strength of its distribution network and an increased market share occasioned by the lower availability of gem diamonds from other sources".
The group said it expected second half sales to be lower, "reflecting the usual relationship between first and second half sales".

It described retail demand in Europe as mixed, with the UK and Germany showing rising sales but French and Italian sales as sluggish. Global retail sales, expressed in dollars, were down marginally in 1996 because of a weaker yen against the dollar.
"I think that (Europe) is likely to continue (the same as the first half. We would hope that overall Europe would be slightly up on the year as a whole," said Capon.

De Beers' market share gained ground on restrained Russian exports, due to licensing delays; reduced activity in Angola due to higher rainfall and the security situation and due to disruption of supplies in the Democratic Republic of Congo or former Zaire.
The group, which controls about 75 percent of the $4.5 billion annual world trade in uncut diamonds, said that the U.S., its largest market, was continuing to grow at a similar rate to last year.

Capon told Reuters that De Beers has been told that the long-delayed trade deal with Russia should come through this month. Russia and De Beers have been in talks about a new trade deal for over two years.
"The delay is essentially a question of the internal debate in Russia as to the future direction of its diamond industry and has not yet been resolved into a final decision," said Capon.
